title: The puzzle of misinformation: Exposure to unreliable content in the United States is higher among the better informed
screen_reason: Observational web-tracking panel (Nielsen, N ~ 140,000 US desktop users, Jan-Dec 2018) with a domain-list definition of unreliable sources. It reports a verbatim concentration statistic (top 1% of panelists = 65.3% of all unreliable pages visited) and a verbatim share of panelists who are heavy consumers of unreliable content (about 1% visit >= 100 unreliable pages). Both are quantitative shares with stated denominators drawn from behavioural data, so the paper is eligible.

estimates.measure_type: top 1% of panelists (by number of unreliable pages visited) account for 65.3% of all unreliable pages visited by the panel
estimates.value_raw: 1% of the panelists are responsible for visiting 65.3% of the pages [unreliable news]
estimates.conc_group_label: top 1% of panelists by number of unreliable news pages visited (N ~ 1,400 panelists, each visiting at least 100 unreliable pages)
estimates.denominator: all unreliable-source page visits made by the ~140,000 US panelists over the 12 months (visits to the 504 unreliable domains visited at least once)
estimates.definition: Pages counted as unreliable if the parent domain is on the merged unreliable list: the 510-domain misinformation list of Grinberg et al. (2019) plus NewsGuard 2018 red-rated domains (trust score < 60); 504 such domains were visited at least once.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Websites with a score <60 points receive a red rating, which means that they are deemed to generally fail to meet basic standards of credibility and transparency and can be considered as unreliable sources"
estimates.n: ~140,000 panelists (136,054 with demographic data); 504 unreliable domains visited
estimates.source_quote: Still, N ~ 1400 panelists (about 1%) visit at least 100 unreliable news pages during our observation period. This 1% of the panelists are responsible for visiting 65.3% of all unreliable pages in our data; by contrast, 1% of the panelists make up for 43.2% of all the reliable news pages visited during our observation window. Exposure to unreliable content is thus more concentrated and skewed than exposure to reliable news content.
estimates.page_loc: Results/Variables section p. 1533 (also stated verbatim in the Figure 1 caption, p. 1532)
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Two pre-existing source lists merged: Grinberg et al. (2019) misinformation domain list (itself built from BuzzFeed, PolitiFact, FactCheck.org, Snopes and prior research) and NewsGuard 2018 trust scores (<60 = red). No new human coding; the authors report 58/69 (84%) overlap between the two lists as evidence of convergence; no kappa.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our data track web browsing behavior for N ~ 140,000 unique users in the United States for the period of January-December 2018. The data are provided by Nielsen, the media measurement company, and it is weighted to be representative of the US population.
estimates.notes: conc_unit = user, conc_dimension = exposure (page visits, i.e. consumption, not sharing). The companion figure for RELIABLE news (top 1% = 43.2% of news pages) is not a misinformation estimate and is not extracted. unit coded 'exposure' because the share is a share of page visits, while the group is defined over persons.

estimates.measure_type: % of panelists who visited at least 100 unreliable news pages during the 12-month window (heavy-exposure threshold, NOT at-least-once reach)
estimates.value_raw: N ~ 1400 panelists (about 1%) visit at least 100 unreliable news pages
estimates.denominator: ~140,000 US panelists tracked in the Nielsen desktop web panel, January-December 2018
estimates.definition: Panelist visited >= 100 pages from the 504 unreliable domains (Grinberg et al. 2019 misinformation list + NewsGuard red-rated 2018 domains) during the 12-month observation window.
estimates.misinfo_def: "Websites with a score <60 points receive a red rating, which means that they are deemed to generally fail to meet basic standards of credibility and transparency and can be considered as unreliable sources"
estimates.source_quote: Still, N ~ 1400 panelists (about 1%) visit at least 100 unreliable news pages during our observation period.
estimates.page_loc: p. 1533 (repeated in Discussion, p. 1538: "only 1% of our panelists visit at least 100 unreliable pages")
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Merged Grinberg et al. (2019) + NewsGuard (<60) domain lists; no human coding of individual pages; no reliability statistic.
estimates.moderator_quote: For each panelist we then count the number of pages from unreliable sources visited in each month, as well as the time spent on those pages (in seconds).
estimates.notes: FLAG FOR ADJUDICATOR: this is a >= 100-pages threshold, NOT the usual 'exposed at least once' reach. It must not be pooled with at-least-once reach estimates; borderline=true and definition_variant=true mark it. The at-least-once figure is NOT extractable per R8: the paper states only the negative side ('the vast majority, that is ~79%, do not visit any page classified as unreliable'), so any at-least-once reach (~21%) would be a complement I computed. Value is approximate in the source ('about 1%').

missed_or_uncertain: (1) At-least-once reach is stated only as its complement: "the vast majority, that is ~79%, do not visit any page classified as unreliable (again, confirming the finding that misinformation affects a small fraction of the online population)". R8 forbids keeping a complement I compute, so no ~21% reach row was created. If the review's rule allows absence-numerator conversion, this is the single most valuable number in the paper (~79% zero-exposure among ~140,000 US desktop panelists, 2018). (2) Likewise "~41% of the panelists do not visit any news page" is about news generally, not misinformation. (3) Instrument-overlap statistics are not prevalence and were not extracted: "Only 199 of these 510 domains (39%) were visited by our panelists at least once" and "Among the 69 misinformation outlets that are identified by Grinberg et al. (2019), visited by our panelists, and rated by NewsGuard, 58 of them (84%) have credibility scores <60". (4) The reliable-news concentration figure (top 1% = 43.2% of news pages) is a reliable-content statistic, not misinformation. (5) No diet-share number is reported: Figures 1(c), 1(d), 2 and 3 are distributions and mixed-effects coefficients with no percentages in the text, and the share of the average news diet that is unreliable is never given. (6) Time-spent exposure is described only qualitatively ("there is also less engagement with unreliable news compared with reliable sources when engagement is measured as time spent"). (7) Demographic predictors are reported as model coefficients only (Figure 3, Supplemental Tables A1-A4), never as subgroup shares.

rob.design: Observational desktop web-browsing panel supplied by Nielsen: N ~ 140,000 unique US users, January-December 2018, URL-level logs plus demographics (136,054 panelists in the demographic table), weighted by Nielsen to be representative of the US population; half of panelists active >= 4 months, ~16,000 active all 12 months; no response rate or attrition model; misinformation identified purely by domain list (Grinberg et al. 2019 510 domains, of which 199 visited, merged with NewsGuard 2018 red ratings <60, total 504 unreliable domains visited), no human coding and no inter-coder reliability; analysis by linear mixed-effects models with panelist ID and month as random effects; acknowledged limits: desktop only (no mobile), URL-level only (no in-platform/visual misinformation), US-only, correlational.
rob.item6_quote: Websites with a score <60 points receive a red rating, which means that they are deemed to generally fail to meet basic standards of credibility and transparency and can be considered as unreliable sources, consistent with prior research (e.g. Aslett et al., 2022).
rob.item10_quote: Still, N ~ 1400 panelists (about 1%) visit at least 100 unreliable news pages during our observation period. This 1% of the panelists are responsible for visiting 65.3% of all unreliable pages in our data.
